![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222769/assets/5034bb902aadd151cc1a28764e054dbdd6a694ad653f50557e5fc208c8ec2342.png)

Find the arc length of the polar curve $r=1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ for $0\le \theta \le \pi $ (shown in blue in the diagram above).

*Hint: You may wish to use the following identity: $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})=\sqrt{\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall the identity for $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2}):$

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})=\sqrt{\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}}
$$

Using $x=\theta $ in the above identity, the integral can be rewritten as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={2\cdot 2(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2}))|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =4(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =4(1-0) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We need to use integration by parts. 

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u={x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({x}^{2})(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1))-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)-2\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we use integration by parts to evaluate $\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1 \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(x)(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1))-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1))(1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)+\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)\,\text{d}x & ={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)-2(-x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)+D) \\  & ={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)-2D \\  & =({x}^{2}-2)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-1)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-2D.$

questions.problem:
The total amount of money $M(t)$ in a charity’s fundraising account $t$ days after the first day of a campaign is given by the function

$$
M(t)=1500+{\int }_{0}^{t}(3{x}^{2}-27)\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $M$ is measured in dollars, and $t\ge 0$ is the time (in days) since the first day of the campaign.

Find the time when the total amount is minimum, and how much money was in the account at that time.

The minimum amount is
$$$
{{field-1}}
after 
{{field-2}} days.
questions.worked_solution:
To find when the total amount is a minimum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}M}{\text{d}t}=0.$ First, we differentiate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}M}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1500+{\int }_{0}^{t}(3{x}^{2}-27)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1500)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({\int }_{0}^{t}(3{x}^{2}-27)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{\int }_{0}^{t}(3{x}^{2}-27)\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{t}^{2}-27\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve $\frac{\text{d}M}{\text{d}t}=0$:

$$
3{t}^{2}-27=0\,⇒\,t=3
$$

So there are two candidates for global extrema, $t=0$ and $t=3.$ To find out how much money is in the account when $t=3,$ we figure out $M(3)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}M(3) & =1500+{\int }_{0}^{3}(3{x}^{2}-27)\,\text{d}x \\  & =1500+[{x}^{3}-27x]{|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =1500+[({3}^{3}-27(3))-(0)] \\  & =1500+[27-81] \\  & =1500-54 \\  & =1446\end{aligned}
$$

Since $1446<1500$, we conclude that the minimum amount is $$\,1446$, and this will happen after $3$ days.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222769/assets/5806f57e41eeb5548b0c041533adf3952dd7f35236121f9056c57f03c2854ddc.png)

Consider the arc of the curve $y=\sqrt{1-x}$ that lies in the first quadrant between $x=0$ and its $x$-intercept. What integral gives the area of the surface generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $x$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1-x} & =0 \\ 1-x & =0 \\ x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=1.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{1-x})=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1-x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}x\sqrt{1+{(-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1-x}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}x\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4(1-x)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}x\sqrt{\frac{5-4x}{4(1-x)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}x\sqrt{\frac{4x-5}{x-1}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A population of $50\,000\,000$ people is being vaccinated against a disease. The rate of growth in the number of people $P(t)$ vaccinated is jointly proportional to the number of people who have been vaccinated at time $t,$ measured in months, and the number of unvaccinated people. If the constant of proportionality is $0.3,$ which differential equation could be used to model $P(t)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the growth rate of vaccinated people is *jointly* proportional to the number of people who have been vaccinated at time $t,$ and the number of unvaccinated people, the number of vaccinated people follows a logistic growth model.

A logistic growth equation has the form

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=kP(a-P),
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>P$ is the carrying capacity.

In this case, the constant of proportionality is $k=0.3,$ and the carrying capacity is $a=50\,000\,000.$ Therefore, the number of people who have been vaccinated is given by the equation

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=0.3P(50\,000\,000-P).
$$
